title: Social and Political Perspectives in the Constituent Assembly

cards.b:
The Constituent Assembly sat for 2 years, 11 months and 18 days (December 1946 to November 1949). It held 11 sessions and about 165 sittings. Its debates, published in 12 volumes, are the best record of what the framers meant.

For UPSC, the focus is not just on process but on ideas. Who sat in the Assembly? Whose voices were heard, whose absent? Where did members disagree: on the strength of the Centre, language, minority rights, property, socialism, the village, and the place of religion?

This lesson maps those disagreements. It uses Granville Austin's classic work as the base: the Constitution as a "seamless web" of three strands, national unity, democracy and a social revolution. Link this lesson with the Preamble, Directive Principles and federalism later.

• Set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946). Members were indirectly elected by provincial legislatures (themselves chosen on a limited franchise). The plan allotted 389 seats: 296 for British India and 93 for princely states.
  • The Congress won a large majority in the 1946 elections (208 of 296 British Indian seats), with the Muslim League 73.
  • After Partition, membership fell to about 299.
  • Dr Rajendra Prasad was President. B.N. Rau was Constitutional Adviser. The Drafting Committee had seven members, with Ambedkar as chair.
  • The Constitution had 395 Articles and 8 Schedules when adopted.

• Leaders and lawyers: Nehru, Patel, Rajendra Prasad, Maulana Azad, K.M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, B.N. Rau (adviser), T.T. Krishnamachari.
  • Ambedkar: elected from Bengal, then from Bombay after Partition, with Congress help.
  • Tribal voices: Jaipal Singh Munda argued for tribal rights and was heard in the Fifth and Sixth Schedule debates.
  • Women: 15 members, among them Hansa Mehta, Durgabai Deshmukh, Sarojini Naidu, Vijayalakshmi Pandit, Renuka Ray, Sucheta Kripalani, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, Begum Aizaz Rasul, Ammu Swaminathan, Dakshayani Velayudhan.
  • Other voices: Muslim League members (to 1947), Anglo-Indians (Frank Anthony), Sikhs (Hukam Singh), a few communists (Somnath Lahiri) and socialists (K.T. Shah), and princely state representatives.

Critics: not chosen by universal franchise; Congress dominated; few Dalit, tribal and women members. Austin replies that Congress itself contained many views, so debate was real.

cards.h: The Objectives Resolution and the guiding vision
cards.b:
On 13 December 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution. It was adopted on 22 January 1947 and is the source of the Preamble.

  • India to be an independent sovereign republic.
  • A Union of territories with autonomous units and residuary powers.
  • All power derived from the people.
  • Justice, equality and freedom for all, and safeguards for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and depressed classes.

Nehru said it was a declaration, a pledge and a dedication. It sought the middle path between Western liberal democracy and Soviet-style socialism.

Austin's three strands: national unity and integrity, democratic government, and a social revolution to end hunger, inequality and caste. The framers saw all three as one "seamless web".

cards.h: Centre and states: a strong Union
cards.b:
• Partition, riots and the integration of over 500 princely states pushed the framers to a strong Centre.
  • Article 1: India, that is Bharat, is a Union of States. Ambedkar explained that the Union is indestructible, and that states cannot secede, unlike in a compact between states.
  • The Constitution has a federal structure with unitary features: Seventh Schedule lists, Governors, Article 356, All-India Services and single citizenship. K.C. Wheare called it "quasi-federal".
  • Dissent: members from the South and from smaller states feared domination. Some wanted a looser union.
  • Special cases: Article 370 for Jammu and Kashmir (draft Art. 306A, accepted in October 1949; abrogated in August 2019) and Articles 371 onwards for other states.

cards.h: Language: Hindi, English and the regions
cards.b:
Language was the most heated argument of 1949. Hindi supporters (Purushottam Das Tandon, Seth Govind Das, R.V. Dhulekar) wanted Hindi as the national language. Members from non-Hindi regions, such as T.T. Krishnamachari, warned of "Hindi imperialism".

The outcome was the Munshi-Ayyangar formula (September 1949):

  • Hindi in the Devanagari script as the official language of the Union (Article 343), not "national language".
  • English to continue for 15 years (till 1965), with Parliament able to extend.
  • Regional languages in the Eighth Schedule (14 at first, 22 now).
  • Article 351 directs the Union to promote Hindi.

The compromise led to the Official Languages Act 1963 and the anti-Hindi agitations in Tamil Nadu (1965).

• Separate electorates were a legacy of 1909. After Partition, most Muslim and Sikh members agreed to drop them. Sardar Patel, chair of the Advisory Committee on Minorities, argued for a united nation.
  • The Assembly accepted joint electorates with reserved seats for SC and ST (Articles 330, 332). Reservation for religious minorities was dropped in May 1949.
  • Rights of minorities were kept through Articles 25-30.
  • Secularism: no state religion, equal respect for all faiths. The word "secular" was added to the Preamble in 1976, and K.T. Shah's attempts to insert "secular" and "socialist" were rejected in 1948.
  • Religion and reform: debates on cow protection (ended as Directive Principle, Article 48) and on a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44, again a Directive Principle; Muslim members objected).

cards.h: Rights, property and the social revolution
cards.b:
• Fundamental Rights versus Directive Principles: B.N. Rau and the Sapru Committee split rights into justiciable and non-justiciable. Social-economic aims went into Part IV. Ambedkar called the Directive Principles an "instrument of instructions" for governments.
  • Property: the hardest compromise. Nehru and the socialists wanted zamindari abolition and compensation fixed by Parliament. Patel and conservatives wanted full compensation. The result was Article 31, soon amended (First Amendment 1951, Ninth Schedule).
  • Socialism: K.T. Shah and the Left wanted a socialist state. The majority preferred a mixed economy. The Directive Principles (Articles 38, 39) carry the egalitarian aim.
  • Untouchability: abolished by Article 17 with little dissent.
  • Preventive detention (Article 22) was fiercely debated. Critics, such as Hriday Nath Kunzru, objected.

• Gandhian: Shriman Narayan's Gandhian Constitution for Free India (1946) and members like K. Santhanam and K. Hanumanthaiya wanted a base of village panchayats. The result: Article 40 as a Directive Principle, and constitutional status only in 1992.
  • Socialist and Marxist: K.T. Shah, Somnath Lahiri. The Constitution protected property and had an elite-led process.
  • Federal/regional: smaller states and regions wanted more powers.
  • Hindu traditionalists: some sought a basis in ancient institutions and Hindu values, such as cow protection. Others, like the Hindu Mahasabha later, criticised the Constitution.
  • Dalit: Dalit members joined the debate on safeguards; Dakshayani Velayudhan insisted on real equality.

The Assembly rarely voted; Austin notes the habit of reaching consensus through accommodation.

On the last day of debate, Ambedkar gave three warnings.

  1. Grammar of anarchy: now that constitutional methods exist, give up unconstitutional methods such as civil disobedience, non-cooperation and satyagraha.
  2. Hero worship: do not lay your liberties at the feet of any great man. Bhakti may be a path to salvation in religion, but in politics it leads to dictatorship.
  3. Social democracy: political democracy cannot last unless it rests on social democracy, which recognises liberty, equality and fraternity as principles of life.

He also pointed to the contradiction in the republic being born: equality in politics, but inequality in social and economic life. In his words, we must remove it soon or those who suffer inequality will blow up the structure of political democracy. He added that without fraternity, equality and liberty would be no deeper than coats of paint.

• Constitution Day: 26 November has been observed since 2015. The 75th anniversary in 2024-25 brought special Parliament debates, in December 2024.
  • Reading the debates: courts cite the Constituent Assembly Debates to interpret provisions. Recent debates about the "basic structure", the Preamble (see Balram Singh, 2024) and federal balance often go back to them.
  • Unfinished agenda: Article 44 (UCC), language policy, women's representation (106th Amendment, 2023) and the status of Governors.
  • Legitimacy question: Today's critics ask whether an indirectly elected Assembly could speak for all, while defenders point to its pluralism and to long continuity.
  • Global view: the Assembly is cited as a model of a deliberative process in a deeply divided society (see lesson 0-5-3).

"The Indian Constitution is a 'seamless web' of national unity, democracy and social revolution." Discuss.
Discuss the social and political perspectives in the Constituent Assembly.
Examine the debates on language, federalism and minority rights in the Constituent Assembly.
What are the main criticisms of the Constituent Assembly? Are they valid?

Structure: set the context in short: composition and timeline. Present Austin's three strands. Then take 4 to 5 debates (Centre-states, language, minorities, property and DPSP, village), each with who argued what and the compromise reached. Add Ambedkar's closing speech for depth. Evaluate with critics' points and the later record of the Constitution.

quiz.q: The Constituent Assembly held its first meeting on…
quiz.w: Sachchidananda Sinha was the temporary chair; Rajendra Prasad was elected President two days later.

quiz.q: The Objectives Resolution was moved by…
The Drafting Committee was chaired by…
Granville Austin's book on the Constitution is titled…
quiz.w: The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation (1966).

quiz.q: Which three strands does Austin identify?
quiz.w: He sees them as a seamless web.

quiz.q: Under the Munshi-Ayyangar formula, English was to continue for…
Article 343 makes which language the official language of the Union?
quiz.w: Hindi is the official, not the national, language.

quiz.q: Who chaired the Advisory Committee on Minorities?
quiz.w: Patel steered the dropping of separate electorates.

quiz.q: In his 25 November 1949 speech, 'grammar of anarchy' refers to…
quiz.w: Ambedkar urged citizens to give them up under the new constitutional order.

quiz.q: Constitution Day (26 November) has been observed since…
quiz.w: Declared in 2015, around Ambedkar's 125th birth anniversary.

Constituent Assembly Debates (12 volumes), including Ambedkar's speech of 25 November 1949
